newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sets new sugar quota, formula for revisions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sets new sugar quota, formula for revisions.

text.p: The U.S. import quota for sugar will be 2.3 million metric tons for fiscal 1997, said the Agriculture Department Friday, while adopting a unique formula to decide whether to adjust the quota.
The tariff-rate quota for fiscal 1997, which opens this Oct. 1, is slightly higher than the 2.17 million tons approved for the current fiscal year.
U.S. imports are restricted as part of a federal programme that assures a minimum price to domestic growers.

Growers and processors generally welcomed a formula that spelled out how alterations would be decided. But, each side had looked for changes that would give it an advantage. Growers wanted lower imports, which would boost prices, while processors wanted assurance of ample supplies.
Under the new formula, sugar-growing nations will be given initial allocations totalling 1.7 million tons. Additional increments of 200,000 tons each will be considered in January, March and May.
If the projected stocks outweigh use by less than 15.5 percent, another 200,000 tons would be allocated. If the ratio of stocks to use is above 15.5 percent, the quota would not be changed.
An announcement was expected Monday of each nation's share of the quota. Brazil, the Philippines, Dominican Republic and Mexico were assured of shares.
With each review, the Agriculture Department would check whether allocations should be reassigned because some nations were unlikely to meet their share.
"I think there will be judgments made on those countries," said Steve Hammond, sugar group leader in the department's Foreign Agricultural Service.
Hammond said the fiscal 1997 quota would result in a 14.3 percent stocks-to-use ratio, based on current data.

The Philippines, Brazil and Dominican Republic will be issued certificates allowing them to ship up to 25 percent of their quota during each quarter of fiscal 1997. Unentered allocations could be carried into the following quarter.

Quota for refined and speciality sugar was set at 47,000 tons but split into three parts -- a speciality sugar quota of 1,656 tons, a most-favoured-nation (MFN) quota of 20,344 tons and an allocation to Mexico of 25,000 tons, which could be filled with refined sugar or raw sugar.
The U.S. trade representative's office was slated to announce later how the MFN quota would be divided. It was available on a first-come, first-served basis this year.
